title: TTree → RNTuple on the ATLAS AF
subtitle: A real Claude Code session that converts 32 GB of analysis ntuples on the UChicago Analysis Facility, entirely through the atlas-af MCP server.

setup.intro: atlas-af is one MCP endpoint in front of the facility's services: ATLAS knowledge search, HTCondor, JupyterHub, Rucio, AMI and more. You log in with your AF account; the gateway acts with your own credentials, so Claude never holds them.

steps.label: Add the server to Claude Code
steps.code: claude mcp add --transport http atlas-af https://mcp.af.uchicago.edu/mcp/

steps.label: Log in
steps.note: Inside Claude Code, pick atlas-af and authenticate with your AF account.

steps.label: Ask in plain language
steps.note: Tools appear as mcp__atlas-af__<service>_<tool>: aos_* searches ATLAS documentation, condor_* drives the batch system, jhub_* drives JupyterHub.

cards.title: One prompt, no recipe
cards.body: The user names the goal and the MCP server, not the tool. Claude has to find out how ATLAS converts TTrees to RNTuple.

cards.title: Tools load on demand
cards.body: The facility exposes many tools. Claude loads only the schemas it needs, here the ATLAS OpenSearch (aos_*) ones.

cards.title: Searching ATLAS, not the web
cards.body: aos_search covers ATLAS documentation, JIRA tickets, GitLab, papers and meeting notes in one index. Each query returns ranked records with the matching passage.

cards.title: Reading the source
cards.body: aos_inspect reads a whole record. Here a production-system ticket gives the exact Merge_tf.py recipe ATLAS used for Open Data, and which release fixed it.

cards.title: Checking what the files really are
cards.body: The benchmarks read flat analysis ntuples, not xAOD, so the right tool is ROOT's RNTupleImporter rather than the Athena transform. One look at the repo settles it.

cards.title: An answer with options
cards.body: The turn ends with both routes, the caveats, and two questions for the user before anything is run.

cards.title: First try: an interactive session
cards.body: condor_interactive_session_* holds a batch slot and runs shell commands in it. Claude reached for it to explore. The user hadn't allowed that mode.

cards.title: The batch pattern
cards.body: condor_submit_job takes a normal submit file. Jobs run on the facility as you, with your own token. Small scripts go up with condor_upload_job_input; the job is released once its inputs arrive.

cards.title: Waiting without polling
cards.body: condor_watch_jobs registers a question ("tell me when this is done"), and condor_check_watches blocks until the answer arrives.

cards.title: A cheap probe first
cards.body: A read-only discovery job reports the input layout (two datasets, 32 GB), confirms the area is writable, and finds ROOT 6.34 with RNTupleImporter in the LCG view.

cards.title: You can steer mid-task
cards.body: Messages typed while Claude works arrive in the same turn. Here the user limits execution to batch jobs or JupyterHub, and Claude switches without losing the work in flight.

cards.title: Trial run on one file
cards.body: 222 MB becomes 60 MB, but only the 43 scalar columns were checked. Claude adds checks for the 197 vector columns before trusting a 3.7× shrink.

cards.title: First real output
cards.body: One file converted into /data next to the originals, with all 240 columns validated: 2 minutes, 1 GB of memory.

cards.title: Fan out
cards.body: One submit, 22 jobs: `queue dataset, idx from (…)` creates one job per remaining file. A single upload call sends the scripts to every job.

cards.title: Independent verification
cards.body: A separate job waits for every output, then checks file counts, entry counts, leftover partial files and compression settings.

cards.title: The result
cards.body: 23/23 files are RNTuple and match their TTrees. The compression settings show the inputs used zlib level 1, so part of the size win comes from compression, not the format.

cards.title: Wrap-up
cards.body: Everything ran on the facility through MCP tool calls: search, batch jobs, file checks. The only local work was writing the scripts that were uploaded.

outro.note: Redacted replay of a real session from 2026-11-15. Internal hostnames, IPs and job identifiers are masked; a side investigation of the facility's own tooling and the follow-up GitHub work are left out; one long tool output in a few places is truncated.
